title: St Brendan's: finding $30 million
prompt: Our client is St Brendan's, a 600-bed non-profit teaching hospital. Its reimbursement rates have been frozen for three years while costs have risen, and the hospital is now running at a deficit. The board has set a target of removing $30 million from an annual cost base of $500 million within two years. The CEO has asked us where that money is going to come from.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Annual cost base by category
Exhibit 2 — Length of stay against benchmark

questions.prompt: Before you start looking for savings, what should you check with the board? Select the two most relevant.
options: Does the $30M have to be a recurring annual reduction, or would one-off savings count?
Are there constraints we must respect — on clinical quality, on compulsory redundancies, on service closures?
How many years has the current CEO been in post?
What is the hospital's bed occupancy rate on a Tuesday?
How does the hospital rank in the national teaching-hospital league table?

optionRationale: A one-off asset sale and a recurring $30M of run-rate are completely different programmes. Settle this first.
In a non-profit provider the constraints are usually what decide which levers are actually available.
Governance colour with no bearing on where $30M comes from.
Far too granular for a framing question, and a single day tells you nothing.
Reputation is not a cost lever.
commonMistakes: Starting to list savings ideas before knowing whether one-off savings count
Ignoring constraints, then recommending redundancies the board has already ruled out

questions.followUp:
On the target: it must be a recurring reduction in the annual run rate, delivered inside two years.

On constraints: no reduction in clinical quality or in the services offered, and no compulsory clinical redundancies. Natural attrition and productivity gains are acceptable.

questions.prompt: How would you go about finding $30 million of cost at St Brendan's? Select the four areas you would work through.
options: Size the cost base by category, so effort goes where the money is
Benchmark clinical and operational performance against comparable hospitals to find the gaps
Separate the price of what the hospital buys from the volume of what it uses
Test each candidate saving against the constraints and against how quickly it can be delivered
Review the hospital's investment portfolio and endowment returns
Assess whether the hospital should merge with a neighbouring provider
Model what reimbursement rates might do in five years' time

optionRationale: The obvious first move, and the one that stops you spending the case on a $25M line.
Benchmarks turn 'we should be more efficient' into a specific, sized gap.
The standard cost decomposition: you can pay less per unit, or use fewer units, and they are different programmes.
The board's constraints and the two-year deadline are what turn a long list into a plan.
Income, not cost, and not the question asked.
A strategic option far beyond a two-year cost programme.
Revenue forecasting, and outside the window.
commonMistakes: Producing a generic cost tree with no way to prioritise between branches
Skipping feasibility, which is where hospital cost programmes actually fail

questions.followUp: Good. Here is the cost base and the one benchmark the finance office has already pulled.

questions.prompt: First, put the target in context. What percentage of the annual cost base is the board asking you to remove?

commonMistakes: Computing the target against a single cost line rather than the total base

questions.followUp:
6% of the run rate in two years. Demanding, but it is the sort of number a provider programme can reach — provided it comes from several places rather than one.

Note what the cost mix says about where to look: staff, facilities and administration together are 75% of the base. Let's start with the benchmark the finance office found.

questions.prompt: Suppose St Brendan's closes its length-of-stay gap to the benchmark, with admissions unchanged. How much would that save annually?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions per year, e.g. 4.5.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Patient-days today: 40,000 admissions × 5.0 days = 200,000.
At the benchmark: 40,000 × 4.6 = 184,000.
Days removed: 16,000.
Saving: 16,000 × $400 variable cost per patient-day = $6.4M a year.
commonMistakes: Applying the $400 to all 200,000 patient-days instead of to the 16,000 removed
Using the total cost per patient-day rather than the variable cost — beds you empty do not save you the fixed cost of the ward
Assuming admissions fall as well; the question holds them constant

questions.followUp:
$6.4M — about 21% of the target from a single operational lever, and one that respects every constraint the board set.

The next largest opportunity is on the buying side.

questions.prompt: Procurement believes it can take 8% out of medical supplies and drugs by renegotiating contracts and standardising the formulary. How much would that contribute?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions per year, e.g. 4.5.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Medical supplies and drugs are 20% of $500M = $100M.
8% of $100M = $8M a year.
commonMistakes: Taking 8% of the whole $500M cost base

questions.followUp: $8M — about 27% of the target, and a price lever rather than a volume one, so it is independent of the length-of-stay work.

questions.prompt: With both of those delivered, how much of the $30M target is still outstanding?

commonMistakes: Double-counting the two levers, which touch different cost lines and are genuinely additive here
Reporting the shortfall as a percentage when the question asks for dollars

questions.followUp: $15.6M outstanding — just over half the target. The two easiest levers get you 48% of the way, which is the usual shape of these programmes: the first half is arithmetic, the second half is management.

questions.prompt: Where should the remaining $15.6M realistically come from? Select the three strongest sources.
options: Staff productivity: rostering, agency and overtime reduction, and natural attrition against the $275M staff line
Administration: consolidating back-office functions and shared services against the $40M line
Facilities and utilities: energy efficiency, estate rationalisation and renegotiated service contracts against the $60M line
Reducing the nursing establishment on every ward by 10%

optionRationale: At $275M it is the only line where a modest percentage — about 5.7% — closes the whole remaining gap, and agency and overtime can move without compulsory redundancies.
Real, though bounded: $40M means even an aggressive programme contributes single-digit millions.
Real and quick: $60M of facilities and utilities is where energy and contract work lands, and none of it touches clinical quality.
Breaches the constraint on service closures, and shifts cost onto neighbouring providers rather than removing it.
A blunt clinical cut that breaches the quality constraint — and the length-of-stay work depends on wards being properly staffed.
A 62% cut to a line nobody has decomposed is a target, not a plan.
commonMistakes: Going after administration first because it feels safe, when $40M cannot carry a $15.6M gap on its own
Proposing clinical cuts that the board has explicitly ruled out
Naming lines without sizing what percentage each would have to give up

questions.followUp:
That is the right shape: the remaining gap has to be spread across the three largest non-clinical-quality levers, with staff productivity carrying most of it at roughly 5.7% of the staff line.

Note the sequencing risk — the length-of-stay saving needs wards staffed well enough to discharge patients promptly, so the staff lever and the length-of-stay lever pull against each other if handled carelessly.

questions.prompt: The board meets in five minutes. Give the CEO your recommendation in six lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the answer: the $30M is reachable, and here is where it comes from
Names the two sized levers first — $6.4M from length of stay, $8M from supplies — as 48% of the target
States the remaining $15.6M and where it comes from: staff productivity, facilities, administration
Quantifies the ask on the largest line: roughly 5.7% of the $275M staff base, via attrition, agency and overtime rather than redundancies
Confirms it respects the board's constraints on quality, services and compulsory redundancy
Names the delivery risk and the next step — the two-year run-rate deadline, and the tension between ward staffing and length of stay
Stays inside six lines and does not narrate the calculation
commonMistakes: Presenting a list of ideas with no numbers attached
Claiming the target is met without accounting for the $15.6M that has no named owner yet
Forgetting that the board asked for a recurring reduction, not a one-off

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.

=== Option checks ===
TRUE  staff at $275M is the only line large enough to carry the remaining $15.6M at a modest percentage: 5.7%
TRUE  admin alone would need a 39% cut -- implausible on its own
FALSE 'other' at $25M would need a 62% cut to carry the remaining $15.6M -- not a credible single source

=== Sanity ===
Target is 6% of the cost base -- demanding but not absurd
Benchmark stay 4.6 days is below current 5.0 but clinically plausible
Two named levers deliver $14.4M of the $30M target
